catalog_quote: Word stress in Papapana is bounded, that is, “main stress is located at a fixed distance from the boundary of the word” (Gussenhoven and Jacobs 1998: 212-213). Secondary stress is not prominent and is an area for further research. There is no lexical stress in Papapana. ... 3.5.1 Regular stress assignment. In Papapana, feet are left-aligned syllabic trochees and word stress is predictable with primary stress falling on the first syllable of the first foot. This differs from canonical Oceanic languages in which stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a word (Lynch et al. 2002: 35). Affixation or cliticisation to either side of the root does not generally alter stress assignment (see §3.5.2 to 3.5.4). Disyllablic monomorphemic roots, such as those in (59)-(63), show that feet in Papapana are trochaic, regardless of whether the syllable nucleus is light or heavy (i.e. whether the syllable contains a monophthong, a long vowel or a diphthong) ... (59) /bɔɾɔ/ ‘pig’ ⟶ [ˈbɔ.ɾɔ] ... Feet consisting of a light syllable followed by a heavy syllable (such as CVCVV or VCVV) demonstrate that stress in Papapana is syllabic or quantity insensitive, meaning syllable weight does not influence foot construction ... (75) /bukaʊ/ ‘dolphin’ ⟶ [ˈbu.kaʊ] *[bu.ˈkaʊ] ... Lexemes consisting of two feet, such as (79)-(83), demonstrate that the leftmost foot carries primary stress and is thus the head foot: (79) /kaβuɾuɾu/ ‘rice’ ⟶ [ˈka.βu.ˌɾu.ɾu]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the (prosodic) word: left-aligned, quantity-insensitive syllabic trochees, leftmost foot is the head, e.g. ['bɔ.ɾɔ] 'pig', ['da.ɾa.mu] 'water', ['ka.βu.ˌɾu.ɾu] 'rice', ['bu.kaʊ] 'dolphin' (not *[bu.'kaʊ]). Stress is entirely predictable; no lexical stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of each subsequent trochaic foot from the left (e.g. ['ka.βu.ˌɾu.ɾu] 'rice', ['gɔ.ɾa.ˌβi.βi] 'vine sp.'), but described as 'not prominent and.. an area for further research' (p. 54); an odd final syllable is extrametrical (['si.nɔ.na] 'bone-3SG.PSSR', p. 58).
new_statements.exceptions: (a) Articles /na, nu/ and subject-indexing proclitics form a phonological but not a prosodic word with the root and are unstressed ([na.'bɔ.ɾɔ]); but if the proclitic fuses with a V-initial root into a long vowel or diphthong the stress falls on the proclitic (["naɪ.nu] 'the house'), and with monosyllabic roots the proclitic forms the foot and is stressed (['na.nɔ] 'the mosquito'), pp. 57-58. (b) Monosyllabic reduplicants are unstressed ([bu.'bu.ɾi.si] 'womb'); when the reduplicant copies a whole foot it takes secondary stress and primary stress stays on the base, so the rightmost foot is the head ([ˌta.mu~'ta.mu] 'food'), p. 56. (c) Some non-synchronically reduplicated forms have irregular second-syllable stress, e.g. /kɔkɔbunu/ 'short' [kɔ.'kɔ.bu.nu], attributed to diachronic reduplication, p. 56. (d) Only five attested CVCVVCV roots, where the medial heavy syllable is unstressed (['tɔ.ɾaː.ɾa] 'axe'), p. 55.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (prosodic word = root plus suffixes/enclitics; proclitics and articles excluded); based on isolated forms and recorded texts, analysed by perception and Praat waveform intensity (p. 54). Same statement repeated nearly verbatim in Smith 2016 Oceanic Linguistics 55(2): 525 (saved file).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Papapana proper (papa1265, ISO ppn), the single variety spoken in Teperoi and neighbouring villages, north-east Bougainville; no dialects distinguished. The 2016 OL article (p. 525) and the 2015 thesis (pp. 54-58) are by the same author on the same fieldwork corpus (2011-2013).

new_statements.identity_note: Papapana as spoken in the Papapana villages of the Autonomous Region of Bougainville (about 106-120 fluent speakers in 2013), documented by Ellen Smith (Smith-Dennis) in fieldwork June 2011-May 2013; the deposit, the 2015 thesis and the 2020 Pacific Linguistics 659 grammar all describe this one variety.
